strengths: EA-KD is simple and potentially useful: its entropy-based weighting introduces no learned parameters or additional inference cost, and Figure 1 reports small absolute training-time overhead.

The visual experiments cover seven distillation frameworks and seven CIFAR-100 teacher–student pairs, alongside Tiny-ImageNet and COCO. Reported improvements include 0.56 percentage points on average in Table 2, 3.39 points over vanilla KD on Tiny-ImageNet, and 0.81/1.68 AP on the two detection configurations.

The manuscript includes relevant ablations of entropy temperature and weighting components, plus training diagnostics and additional GPT-2 experiments. These provide encouraging evidence that entropy weighting can improve distillation.
The central weighting formula is clearly presented, and the datasets and underlying distillation methods are appropriately referenced.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate sample weighting from changes in overall distillation strength. Equations (11)–(14) do not normalize weights to preserve their mean, so EA changes both relative sample contributions and the effective distillation coefficient. Matched constant-weight or shuffled-weight controls and equally tuned baseline coefficients are needed. The reported reduction of the MLD+LS coefficient from 9 to 4 particularly complicates attribution of its 5.48-point Tiny-ImageNet improvement.

The central interpretation of entropy as learning value is insufficiently established. Equations (5)–(7) correctly describe a uniform student, but the high-entropy limiting example has zero KL because teacher and student already agree; entropy weighting leaves that loss zero. This does not demonstrate harmful neglect of useful knowledge. Entropy can also reflect unreliable predictions, while the t-SNE visualizations do not establish actual classifier decision boundaries. The empirical gains support a useful heuristic more strongly than the claimed general explanation.

The distinguishing contribution beyond existing entropy-based and sample-wise weighting approaches remains weakly validated. Related methods such as AKD [13] and RW-KD [22] are discussed, but there is no direct comparison against comparable weighting alternatives. In Table 8, incorporating student entropy improves teacher-only weighting by just 0.07–0.18 percentage points. Without standard deviations or confidence intervals, despite reporting multiple-run averages, the benefit of this adaptive component is uncertain.

Important implementation details are missing. The manuscript does not specify whether student entropy is detached during optimization. Otherwise, differentiating Equation (14) introduces an additional L_KD times gradient-of-weight term, changing the mechanism beyond simply scaling distillation gradients. Detection weighting granularity and token-to-sequence entropy aggregation are also unspecified. The supplement adds visualizations but does not resolve these reproducibility gaps.

Some reporting inconsistencies require correction: EA-KD achieves 75.46 in Table 2 but 75.27 in Table 8 for the stated analysis configuration, and Table 4 reports three runs whereas Section 4.1 says all results use five. These are secondary, correctable issues; the main reasons for weak rejection are the uncontrolled loss-scaling effect and insufficient evidence for the proposed adaptive mechanism.
